notes.meaning: The psalmist calls on God as Israel's Shepherd, asking Him to listen to the cries of His hurting flock. He pictures God sitting on His throne above the golden winged cherubim on the ark of the covenant, the sacred chest where God promised to show mercy. The prayer asks God to let the bright light of His holy presence shine out to guide and protect them.

The prayer asks God to show His mighty strength in front of Ephraim, Benjamin, and Manasseh. During their travels through the wilderness, these three related tribes marched directly behind the sacred ark of God's presence. The writer asks God to rise up as their victorious leader once again and rescue His people from danger.

The people plead with God to restore them and to look on them with a welcoming, smiling face. They know that only God's personal favor can bring true rescue and safety. If the Lord turns toward them in mercy, all their troubles can be set right.

differ.view: John Calvin explained this as a simple prayer for God to restore the nation to its former outward peace and safety rather than an inward spiritual change.
John Gill and Charles Spurgeon held that the prayer primarily asks for converting grace to turn hearts back to God, since true rescue only follows inward repentance.

notes.meaning: The writer asks how long the Lord of all heavenly armies will remain angry while His people are crying out to Him. It brings deep sorrow when God seems to turn away even from the prayers they offer. The psalmist brings this heavy feeling directly to God, asking why relief has taken so long.

God has given His people sorrow instead of ordinary food, making tears their daily bread. They have been forced to drink down full measures of weeping without relief. Their grief is deep because they recognize that their hardship comes from God correcting them.

Surrounding nations argue over who gets to take advantage of God's weakened people. Unfriendly neighbors look at their misery and laugh among themselves in mockery. It brings great shame to God's people when their painful defeat becomes entertainment for their enemies.

The opening chorus is repeated with greater boldness, now calling on God as the ruler of heavenly armies. The people again ask Him to restore them and turn His shining, friendly face back toward them. They remind themselves that complete rescue depends entirely on His loving favor.

The psalmist compares the nation of Israel to a choice grapevine that God gently dug up and brought out of Egypt. God drove out the pagan nations living in Canaan to clear a safe spot for this special plant. He took a weak and needy people and replanted them where they could grow and flourish.

God prepared the ground by driving away the local peoples and making room for the vine to put down deep roots. Once firmly planted, the nation grew strong and spread across the entire land. This reminds the people how faithfully God cared for them when He first settled them in the promised land.

The vine grew so tall and wide that its leafy shade covered the hills, and its boughs wrapped around the tallest cedar trees. This poetic picture describes how grand and respected Israel became in its best days, especially under King Solomon. God lifted a small nation to great prominence and honor among surrounding lands.

The branches of the vine reached all the way to the Mediterranean Sea on the west and to the Euphrates River on the east. God had completely fulfilled His promise about the broad borders of their homeland. Under His blessing, the influence and trade of the nation reached far beyond its borders.

The writer asks God why He tore down the protective stone walls that guarded the vineyard. Without those walls, every traveler walking by can reach in and strip off the fruit. The people realize that whenever God removes His shield of protection, they are left open to every enemy.

Wild boars and roaming creatures from the woods rush in and tear the tender vines to pieces. These beasts represent cruel foreign nations that marched in and ruined God's people. Without God guarding the borders, a helpless nation is easily crushed and devoured.

The people beg the God of heavenly armies to turn back toward them and look down from heaven. They ask Him not to stay far away, but to come and tend His broken vineyard. When all human help fails, they know that God can still look with pity and bring relief.

The prayer asks God to protect the root that His own strong right hand planted long ago. It also asks Him to care for the branch, or son, that He raised up and made strong for His own purpose. The people plead that God will not let the work He began with so much love be completely destroyed.

The vineyard has been cut down with axes and burned with fire like useless brush. The writer confesses that the people are perishing under God's angry rebuke, not merely by the strength of human foes. They know that God's displeasure is the real cause behind all their ruin.

The psalmist asks God to place His strengthening hand on the man at His right hand, whom He raised up for Himself. In its first setting, this was a prayer for the Davidic king who was called to lead and protect God's people. Ultimately, Christians understand this title as pointing to Jesus the Messiah, whom God exalted to His right hand to save the world.

differ.view: John Calvin explained the phrase as describing the whole nation of Israel, whom God had chosen and strengthened as a single corporate son, rather than speaking directly of a king or the Messiah.
Adam Clarke taught that the title belongs fully and properly only to Jesus the Messiah, the true intercessor standing at God's right hand to reconcile sinners to God.

notes.meaning: If God upholds and strengthens His chosen leader, the people promise never to turn back to idols or disobedience. They ask God to revive them with fresh spiritual life so they can worship and pray with honest hearts. Only God's renewing power can keep His people faithful to Him.

The psalm closes by repeating the main plea a third time, now using the full personal name, the LORD God of hosts. The people ask once more for God to restore them and let His friendly face shine down upon them. A single glance of God's favor is all they need to be completely saved.
